beats.title: Supply and Demand
beats.teacherMove: introduce the market as the meeting place between buyers and sellers
beats.script: Welcome in. Today we are going to make supply and demand feel like something you can actually see, not just a graph in a textbook. Think of a market stall: buyers arrive with wants, sellers arrive with goods, and the price helps both sides decide what to do. We will start with the two laws, then look at real scenes where those laws show up. By the end, the graph should feel like a map of real behavior.

ops.prompt: busy produce marketplace with buyers, sellers, and visible goods changing hands, cinematic documentary photo, no text

beats.title: Law of Demand
beats.teacherMove: explain the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded
beats.definitionMeaning: How much buyers are willing and able to buy at different prices.
beats.script: The law of demand says that, other things equal, people usually buy more when the price is lower. A lower price makes the good easier to justify, so more buyers enter and existing buyers may buy extra units. When price rises, some buyers step back or switch to something else. That is why the demand curve slopes downward.

ops.text: Rule: move along one demand curve

beats.title: Law of Supply
beats.teacherMove: explain the direct relationship between price and quantity supplied
beats.definitionMeaning: How much sellers are willing and able to offer at different prices.
beats.script: The law of supply runs the other direction. When the price is higher, sellers have a stronger reason to produce, stock, or bring more units to market. When price falls, the reward is weaker, so some sellers cut back or stop offering as much. That is why the supply curve slopes upward.

ops.text: Rule: move along one supply curve

beats.title: Demand in a Market
beats.teacherMove: connect demand to buyer behavior in a concrete market scene
beats.script: Now let’s attach the demand law to a real scene. Look at the buyers gathered around the tomatoes: that crowd is not abstract demand, it is people deciding whether the good is worth it to them. If the price becomes easier to accept, more hands reach in and more units leave the crate. The graph is just a clean way to summarize that behavior.

ops.prompt: open-air produce market tomato stall with seller, buyers reaching, full crates, and a quieter produce section, cinematic documentary photo, no text

beats.title: Supply Behind the Stall
beats.teacherMove: show supply as production choices before goods reach the market
beats.script: Supply starts before the product reaches the stall. In a bakery, flour, labor, ovens, and time all shape how many loaves can be offered. If the selling price rises or production becomes easier, the bakery has a reason to send more bread out. If costs rise, the same bakery may supply less at every price.

ops.prompt: small bakery production room with flour sacks, oven, bakers, cooling racks, and delivery crates, cinematic documentary photo, no text

beats.title: Why Demand Shifts
beats.teacherMove: use a grocery choice scene to explain demand shifters
beats.script: A shift in demand is different from moving along the same demand curve. The price of this good is not the only thing changing the decision. A new trend, a change in income, a substitute product, or a complementary item can make people want more or less at every possible price. That is why the whole demand curve moves.

ops.prompt: grocery aisle with shoppers choosing between similar products, basket with complementary goods, and a competing shelf, photorealistic retail scene, no text

beats.title: Shifts in Demand
beats.teacherMove: summarize demand shifters on a written board
beats.definitionMeaning: A change in demand at every price, caused by something other than the good's own price.
beats.script: Let’s now write the demand shifters cleanly. Income can push demand right for normal goods. Tastes and trends can also move the curve because people now value the good differently. Substitutes and complements matter because goods are connected in everyday choices.

ops.text: Rule: non-price factor moves the curve

beats.title: Shifts in Supply
beats.teacherMove: summarize supply shifters on a written board
beats.definitionMeaning: A change in supply at every price, caused by production conditions.
beats.script: Supply shifts when the conditions of production change. Lower costs or better technology let sellers offer more at the same price, so supply shifts right. Higher input prices, taxes, or disruptions make production harder, so supply shifts left. Again, this is not just sliding along the curve; the whole curve moves.

ops.text: Rule: production conditions move the curve

beats.title: Equilibrium
beats.teacherMove: show supply and demand meeting at a market-clearing point
beats.script: Now we can put the two curves on the same graph. Demand slopes down, supply slopes up, and the crossing point is equilibrium. At that price, the quantity buyers want matches the quantity sellers want to offer. If the price is away from that point, pressure builds to move it back.

beats.title: Checkpoint: Demand
beats.teacherMove: check whether the student can identify movement along demand
beats.script: Quick checkpoint. What usually happens to quantity demanded when the price of a good decreases, assuming other things stay the same?

checkpoint.prompt: When price decreases, what usually happens to quantity demanded?
checkpoint.correctFeedback: Exactly. Lower price usually increases quantity demanded.
checkpoint.hintFeedback: Think about buyers: if it becomes cheaper, are they usually willing to buy more or less?
checkpoint.revealAnswer: Quantity demanded usually increases when price decreases.

beats.title: Market Dynamics
beats.teacherMove: animate how a shock moves through the market
beats.script: Markets are dynamic because one change can move through the whole system. Imagine production gets cheaper: supply shifts right, sellers bring more units, and the old price may now be too high. Competition puts downward pressure on price until buyers and sellers settle into a new balance. The movement is not random; it follows the pressure created by surplus or shortage.

beats.title: Final Checkpoint
beats.teacherMove: check whether the student can distinguish a shift from movement along a curve
beats.script: Final checkpoint. If a new technology makes bread cheaper to produce, is that mainly a movement along the supply curve or a shift of the supply curve?

checkpoint.prompt: New technology makes production cheaper. Is that movement along supply, or a supply shift?
checkpoint.correctFeedback: Yes. Technology changes production conditions, so the supply curve shifts.
checkpoint.hintFeedback: Ask whether the good's own price changed, or whether production conditions changed.
checkpoint.revealAnswer: It is a supply shift, usually to the right.

beats.title: Supply and Demand Recap
beats.teacherMove: close with a written recap of the core logic
beats.script: Let’s close by locking in the whole map. Demand is the buyer side: lower price usually means more quantity demanded. Supply is the seller side: higher price usually means more quantity supplied. Shifts happen when something besides the good's own price changes the whole relationship. Equilibrium is the place where buyer plans and seller plans match.
